REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT

[
1
]

In the fall of 1995, after ten years of marriage, Lynne Cheryl Katz
and Menachem Nimelman separated.  They dealt with some of the issues arising
out of the separation by way of agreement.  They sold their matrimonial home
and shared the proceeds equally.  They agreed to their two young sons living
with Ms. Katz and on the amount of child support that Mr. Nimelman would pay.
They made some attempts to come to a final agreement, but were unsuccessful.

[
2
]

At the end of 2001, Ms. Katz issued a petition for divorce and
corollary relief. This resulted in further negotiations; however, they ended in
2002 with no agreement in place.  Over the next few years, Ms. Katz and Mr.
Nimelman focused their energies on their children with very little being done
to arrive at a final agreement.  That changed in January 2005 as a result of
Oren, their eldest son moving in with Mr. Nimelman.  Since then, Ms. Katz and Mr.
Nimelman have been engaged in acrimonious and costly litigation.

[
3
]

The issues to be determined are Mr. Nimelman`s entitlement to an
equalization payment and the amount of that payment if there is a finding of
entitlement; Ms. Katz`s entitlement to spousal support; the amount of child
support payable by Mr. Nimelman; and, the obligation to pay the extraordinary
expenses of the children.

BACKGROUND

[
4
]

Ms. Katz is 53 years old.  She is a lawyer, first called to the bar
in Manitoba and subsequently in Ontario.  Since 1998, she has been on a disability pension.  Although the
parties have agreed only that she has been disabled since 2005, Mr. Nimelman
did not argue that she should have been employed between 1998 and 2005.

[
5
]

According to Ms. Katz, the disability is progressive and arises
out of a neurological condition affecting co-ordination and balance and causing
constant muscular pain and extreme fatigue.  Ms. Katz’s evidence is that it
also has a mental element which results in her having difficulty dealing with
numbers.  She has physiotherapy several times a week and regular massage to
control her symptoms.  At trial, she walked with a cane.  There is no medical
evidence with respect to her condition.  Its impact on her is discussed in
further detail below.

[
6
]

Mr. Nimelman is 54 years old.  He is an aeronautical engineer
trained in Israel where he was
born.  He has been employed by MDA Space Missions in Brampton since 1991.  His expertise is in a highly specialised area of
aeronautical engineering.  His employment is not secure.  The company has been
reliant on U.S. projects but
there have been no new projects since 2004.  There have been layoffs in the
company and the division for which he works is up for sale.  Mr. Nimelman is
working with the company in an effort to develop new business, seeing this as
holding the best prospect for him as employment at another company would mean a
reduction in income because there is no Canadian company engaged in the kind of
work that could take advantage of his expertise.

[
7
]

Ms. Katz and Mr. Nimelman met in Israel in 1983 while Ms. Katz was travelling,  through a mutual friend,
Penny Goldberg. They moved in together some months later and married in March
1985.  During this time, Ms. Katz wrote her bar admission exams in Israel and began articling.  Her income was
modest and she was supported by Mr. Nimelman.

[
8
]

Soon after marrying, the couple decided to move to Canada, believing that their economic
prospects would be better here.  The intention was to stay for just a few
years.  The undisputed evidence is that Mr. Nimelman agreed to the move only on
condition that they would return to Israel regularly so that he could see his family with whom he was very
close. They left Israel in the
spring of 1986.

[
9
]

Ms. Katz set about obtaining a call to the Ontario bar, which she accomplished in June 1987.  She began employment
with Baker & McKenzie, practicing labour law.  Until then, she had been
supported by Mr. Nimelman.  Her starting salary was about 50% more than he was
earning and she continued throughout the marriage to earn significantly more
than he earned.

[
10
]

Oren,
their first child, was born in 1988.  By then, they were living in Thornhill.
Noah was born in 1990.  A nanny was hired to provide child care.  They
continued to have a nanny until 1994.

[
11
]

Ms. Katz
left Baker & McKenzie in 1991.  According to Ms. Katz, it was the firm’s
opinion that she was not up to the rigours of private practice.  Although she
did not accept this view, she decided to leave.  According to her, she left out
of a concern that she would not make partner if she stayed.  According to Mr.
Nimelman, however, it was a concern that she was about to be fired that caused
her to take another job.  Ms. Katz accepted a position as executive director
with the firm’s client, the Ontario College of Family Physicians located in Mississauga.

[
12
]

Ms. Katz
says that one of the reasons she left Baker & McKenzie was to spend more
time with their children.  Whether she left of her own accord or was forced to
leave, a result of her departure was that she did work fewer hours as her new
job was only four days a week.

[
13
]

Ms.
Katz’s new position was at a beginning salary of around $77,000.  There is no
evidence as to the amount her earnings at Baker & McKenzie or what a
partner might expect to earn there.  By 1997, when she stopped working, she was
earning $113,000.  Ms. Katz believes she was earning around $107,000 as of
valuation day, which the parties have agreed is September 30, 2005. Despite
being asked to make disclosure, Ms. Katz has not produced any evidence as to
her earnings at that time. Mr. Nimelman’s income in 2005 was $72,230.00.

[
14
]

Ms. Katz
did not return to work following the December 1997 holidays and has not been
employed since then. She maintains that her position with the College was
terminated by the College in February of the next year. She issued a claim
alleging wrongful dismissal against the College and two related claims against
others she claimed to have had a role in her dismissal.

[
15
]

Ms. Katz
was examined for discovery in those actions on a total of 16 days from May 2003
to October 2004.  Seven days of examinations of the defendants were conducted
on her behalf.  The actions were to proceed to trial in November of 2004, but
were adjourned as a result of Ms. Katz’s father being injured.  She had paid
$35,000.00 to her counsel as a retainer for the trial, in October of 2004.  She
subsequently changed counsel.  As of September 2006, the actions had not been
returned to the trial list.

[
16
]

In 1999,
Ms. Katz had offered to settle the actions against the College of Family Physicians for $140,000 plus interest and costs.  It appears that as of
September 2006, there had been no offer from the defendants in any of the three
actions; however, the College had several times offered to mediate, but the
offer was rejected by Ms. Katz. She says that she will assess her situation
regarding these actions once this matrimonial matter is finalilzed.

[
17
]

Ms. Katz
maintains that she bore full responsibility for the care of the children and
the household throughout the marriage.  Mr. Nimelman disputes this, insisting
that he played a significant role.

He
concedes that Ms. Katz drove the children to school in the morning, but that
was because he needed to arrive at work earlier than did she.  In the evenings,
however, he would some times pick the children up from school and, until around
the time of separation when Mr. Nimelman was required to work longer hours
because of a special project in which he was involved at work, he would often arrive
home before Ms. Katz did.  Ms. Katz says that it was the nanny who took care of
the children in the late afternoon and on those occasions when she worked
evenings. Mr. Nimelman disputes this, saying that all the nanny did after he
arrived home from work was help him feed the children.

[
18
]

Ms. Katz
complains that Mr. Nimelman was not involved in the children’s schooling.  The
starting point for this complaint seems to have been the difference in view
between the two as to the reasonableness of Oren attending Bialik, a private
Hebrew day school in mid-town Toronto a considerable distance from the family’s
home, for half-day kindergarten.  Mr. Nimelman was opposed to this because he
believed it would create a logistical nightmare that could not be justified.

[
19
]

The
justification provided by Ms. Katz was that it was the only school that met
their needs and that would allow Oren to learn Hebrew so that he could
communicate with his Israeli grandparents. According to Mr. Nimelman, this view
was unfounded as there were a number of schools in the neighbourhood that would
meet Oren’s needs at that stage of his education.  And, as for Hebrew, it was
Oren’s first language and the language he spoke at home so it was not a
consideration.

[
20
]

Ms. Katz
insisted, nonetheless, on enrolling Oren in Bialik.  Mr. Nimelman could not
take the time from work at lunch to drive from Brampton to pick Oren up and take him home and then return to work.  As a
result, Ms. Katz did all of the driving, which meant a trip from Mississauga at
lunch time to Bathurst and Glencairn, in Toronto and then to Thornhill and the
afternoon program that Oren attended at another Hebrew day school, and then
back to work.

[
21
]

The
following year, Oren attended Bialik full days.  Mr. Nimelman then assisted
with the driving, picking Oren up from Bialik whenever possible.  Meanwhile,
Noah was attending school in Thornhill.

[
22
]

Ms. Katz
claims that she suggested to Mr. Nimelman that they move from Thornhill to the
401 and the Allen Road area to
make the commute easier, but was rebuffed based on Mr. Nimelman’s
self-interest.  Mr. Nimelman adamantly denies that Ms. Katz made any such
proposal.  Oren was still attending Bialik in 1995 when his parents separated.

[
23
]

Ms. Katz
attributes the break-up of the marriage to Mr. Nimelman’s inability to deal
with Oren.  Both parents agree that he was a challenging child: very bright,
hyperactive, defiant and always testing limits. Both clearly are devoted to
Oren and love him very much.  However, Ms. Katz accuses Mr. Nimelman of having
thrown Oren across a room while they were in Israel visiting family in the summer of 1995.  Mr. Nimelman denies the
allegation.  He does say that when Oren’s behaviour became uncontrolled, Mr.
Nimelman would hold Oren until he calmed.  Sometimes it worked, but not
always.  Mr. Nimelman insists that he would never engage in violence against
his children.

[
24
]

Ms. Katz
relies on an e-mail from Oren to Mr. Nimelman sent in April 1995, to
demonstrate that, contrary to Mr. Nimelman’s assertion that he was close to
Oren throughout his childhood, their relationship was strained with the result
that she bore the primary burden of raising Oren.  The e-mail, which is a
complaint by Oren that Mr. Nimelman failed to treat Oren with the respect to
which a 10 year old is entitled and expression of  how very upsetting this was to
Oren, shows him to be precocious and very articulate.  It does not, however, in
the absence of more, demonstrate a troubled relationship between father and
son.  It is consistent with parenting Oren being a challenge, as both parents
agree it was.

[
25
]

The
matrimonial home was sold in May 1996.  The proceeds of the sale were split
equally.  Ms. Katz used hers to buy the home on Blythwood
Avenue where she moved with their two sons and where
she continues to live.  She purchased title to the house only, the land being
leased to her.
[1]
Mr. Nimelman bought a condominium in a building south of the 401
at the Allen Road.

[
26
]

When the
matrimonial home was sold, according to her own evidence, Ms. Katz made a
detailed list of all of the contents of their home “down to the last fork”.
The intention was that they be split equally.  Mr. Nimelman’s evidence is that
he took what he needed and could fit into his condominium, which was much smaller
than the house bought by Ms. Katz, leaving most of the contents for her.

[
27
]

On
separation, Ms. Katz told Mr. Nimelman what he ought to be paying in support
for the children and he continued to pay what was requested until January 2005.

[
28
]

When the
family moved from the matrimonial home, one month was remaining in the school
year.  Ms. Katz takes the position that Mr. Nimelman unilaterally enrolled the
children in a school near his home, which was some distance from Blythwood.
Mr. Nimelman says that the decision was mutual and they together met with the
principal in an attempt to convince him to allow the children to register.
Contrary to what Ms. Katz implied, the location of the school was convenient
for her in spite of its distance from her home as she was able to drop the
children off at the school and continue on to work by way of the Allen Road.
It was Mr. Nimelman who picked the children up from school.

[
29
]

Ms. Katz
does not dispute that she subsequently unilaterally moved Oren to another
Hebrew day school, the Heschel School and did so in spite of Mr. Nimelman saying that he could not afford
to contribute to the cost of private school.  Eventually, Noah attended there
as well.

[
30
]

Both
children experienced increasing problems at Heschel.  Ms. Katz complains of
having been undermined by Mr. Nimelman at the school. For his part, Mr.
Nimelman says that he had to act as a buffer between the school and Ms. Katz to
protect the children.  He received calls from the school administration saying
that they could not work with Ms. Katz. By the summer of 1998, there was a
great deal of friction between her and the school.

[
31
]

Mr.
Nimelman insists that he supported Ms. Katz in his dealings with the school,
believing it important to do so.  He denies that he was responsible for
excluding Ms. Katz from meetings with school representatives, though she
frequently chose to meet with them when he was unavailable.

[
32
]

Ms. Katz
maintains that Mr. Nimelman upset her tremendously by attending a meeting
without her and agreeing to the school’s demand that Oren be maintained on
Ritalin in spite of her belief that Ritalin was counter-indicated.  She points
to this as evidence of behaviour on the part of Mr. Nimelman that was harmful
to her.  However, Mr. Nimelman has a very different version of what occurred
and view of his behaviour towards Ms. Katz.

[
33
]

According
to Mr. Nimelman, at this meeting, he was supportive of Oren’s decision to stop
taking Ritalin and felt that the in demanding that Oren take the medication,
the school was simply trying to take the easy way out.  Ms. Katz reacted demand
by retaining counsel to advance a Human Rights complaint against the school.
Mr. Nimelman supported her in this. (The complaint was settled on the basis of
its being withdrawn in exchange for the Board waiving its claim for costs
against Ms. Katz.)

[
34
]

For the first
two years that the children attended Heschel, Ms. Katz had paid the tuition.
When she did not pay for the year commencing in September 1998, Mr. Nimelman
made arrangements to pay.  Ms. Katz relies on this as further evidence of Mr.
Nimelman behaving in a manner that was intentionally upsetting to her,
maintaining that he unilaterally decided that the children would return to
Heschel.

[
35
]

Mr.
Nimelman disputes that there was any intention on his part to distress Ms.
Katz.  He says that he made arrangements to pay the tuition after being advised
by the school that it was outstanding and after unsuccessfully discussing
alternatives to Heschel with Ms. Katz; he made the arrangements in order to
avoid a crisis for the children.  He confirmed in a letter to Ms. Katz’s lawyer
(sent in response to a letter from her enclosing a draft separation agreement
for Mr. Nimelman’s consideration) why he was doing this and provided specifics
of the accommodations regarding payment the school had made out of recognition
of his financial circumstances.

[
36
]

A few
months into the school year, Oren was asked to leave Heschel.  Noah left soon
after.  Both children were enrolled in a public school. Ms. Katz blames the
challenges they subsequently faced on Mr. Nimelman.

[
37
]

At the
outset, Ms. Katz and Mr. Nimelman tried to settle their outstanding matrimonial
issues through negotiations.  However, finalising an agreement was not their
priority, both of them giving primary importance to trying to respond to the
challenges faced by Noah and Oren following the marriage breakdown. Then, in
December of 2001, Ms. Katz issued a petition for divorce.

[2]
This lead to a case conference in February of 2002, following
which the parties were very close to agreeing on terms of a settlement. But,
finalizing an agreement was put into abeyance pending a decision by Ms. Katz’s
insurer as to the status of her disability benefits. According to Mr. Nimelman,
the delay was also necessitated by the need for further financial disclosure by
Ms. Katz.

[
38
]

There
was very little communication regarding finalizing an agreement for nearly
three years after that.  Neither party pursued relief from the court.  But, the
situation changed suddenly and lastingly in early 2005.  The precipitating
event was Oren’s move to his father’s home.

[
39
]

Ms. Katz
had been experiencing difficulties with Oren.  He was not following the agreed
to rules and was determined to drop a course in which he was doing badly. Ms.
Katz was convinced that this was not in his interests as it was important for
Oren to learn to face his problems rather than run away from them.  The
situation was exacerbated, according to Mr. Nimelman, by Ms. Katz requiring
Oren to move out of the basement apartment and into a bedroom across the hall from
Ms. Katz’s bedroom, to accommodate her niece who had been offered the apartment.
Ms. Katz denies this, but it is confirmed by Penny Goldberg, who had continued
to be Ms. Katz’s close friend until shortly after this time.

[
40
]

Oren,
who was about to turn 17 at the time, and Ms. Katz were in constant conflict
over when Oren went to bed, when he woke, the noise he made and his approach to
school.  At Ms. Katz’s request, Mr. Nimelman tried to intercede but without
success.  The problem, from his perspective was not with the rules Ms. Katz’s
had established for Oren, but rather her failure to apply them in a way that
recognized Oren’s needs given his unique characteristics.  What Mr. Nimelman
did not say, but what appears to have been the case, is that Ms. Katz’s rigid
approach to parenting Oren was counterproductive.

[
41
]

What
happened next is recalled differently by Ms. Katz and Mr. Nimelman.  She says
that when she refused to allow Oren to drop the biology course that he was
failing, he moved in with his father, who then proceeded to allow Oren to drop
the course.  Mr. Nimelman says that he got a call from Ms. Katz saying that she
had kicked Oren out, told him not to come back, did not know where he was and
did not care.

[
42
]

With
some effort, Mr. Nimelman, after receiving this phone call, was able to find
Oren and take him to Mr. Nimelman’s home.  Oren told him that Ms. Katz was so
insistent that he leave immediately that she shut off the water to prevent him
from taking the time to finish the shower he was taking at the time and forced
him out without adequate clothing.  Mr. Nimelman promptly had a meeting at
Oren’s school to discuss his wish drop his biology course.  The advice that Mr.
Nimelman received from the school was that forcing Oren to take the course
would put his entire year at risk.  Oren was allowed to drop the course.

[
43
]

Both
parents agree that the events of early January 2005 traumatized Oren and have
had long term academic and emotional effects on him.  Each holds the other responsible
for the resulting problems Oren has had.

[
44
]

Very soon
after Oren moved in with Mr. Nimelman, he asked Ms. Katz to adjust the child
support payments to reflect the fact that they now had split custody.  His
evidence as to her response is that she refused to consider an adjustment and
told him, with a broad smile on her face, that he could sue if he did not like
it.  Mr. Nimelman then stopped payment on the support cheques that Ms. Katz had
and did not provide her with any others.  He acknowledges that this response
was inappropriate.

[
45
]

In March
2005, Ms. Katz served a notice of motion for interim spousal support and child
support.  The motion was heard in April 2005.  The spousal support aspect of
the motion was dismissed.  Mr. Nimelman was ordered to pay child support for
one child in the amount of $343 dollars based on the parties stated incomes for
2005.  The expectation at the time was that they would have a trial before the
year end.

[
46
]

Ms. Katz
describes what happened subsequently as Mr. Nimelman delaying having the action
tried.  Mr. Nimelman describes it as Ms. Katz making a timely trial impossible
by refusing to comply with her disclosure obligations.

CREDIBILITY

[
47
]

Ms. Katz
and Mr. Nimelman have different recollections of events and different perceptions
as to the significance of those events.  Their evidence differs on critical
issues in the action.  As a result, in deciding the issues before me, I am
required to choose the evidence of one over that of the other.  For the reasons
which follow, unless otherwise noted, I accept Mr. Nimelman’s evidence where
there is a conflict between their evidence.

[
48
]

Ms. Katz
is articulate, obviously intelligent and without question, a devoted mother.  I
accept that she believes her recollection of events to be correct.  However, I
find that those recollections are tainted by her desire to demonstrate the
reasonableness of the positions she has taken and the decisions she has made.

[
49
]

In spite
of a component of her disability being fatigue Ms. Katz showed no signs of tiring
during the trial though she was in the witness stand for the better part of six
days and when not in the stand, sat at the counsel table taking notes and
assisting her counsel.
[3]
While giving evidence, Ms. Katz demonstrated mental agility and
knowledge of the documentary evidence.  It appeared that where she was unable
to recall something, it was because it suited her purposes.

[
50
]

Ms. Katz
did, from time to time appear to have difficulty following questioning that
required her to make any calculations.  She attributes this to her disability
and appears to rely on it as an explanation for her lack of thoroughness in the
completion of her financial statements and her failure to disclose assets.  For
example, she claims that it is as a result of her disability that she did not
disclose that she had $34,000 in Canada Savings Bonds, her disability causing
her to have forgotten that she had the bonds.

[
51
]

I cannot
accept that Ms. Katz was unaware, as she claims to have been, of a number of
investments that she did not disclose.  There being no medical evidence to
support her position that her having forgotten about these assets results from
her disability, I do not accept it.  While it may be that numbers are a “black
hole” for her as she claims, this does not explain her failure to disclose.  I
accept Mr. Nimelman’s position that the inadequacies in her disclosure were
deliberate.

[
52
]

Portions
of Ms. Katz’s evidence simply were not credible.  She gave as her reason for
selling the Bathurst St.
property, an income property that was profitable, the fact that she did not
have the energy to replace the maintenance person when he quit.  While that
does not ring true on its face, it is even less credible given that she
continued to own another building at which she needed similar work to be done.
Its lack of credibility is reinforced by the financial statements with respect
to her properties for the year preceding the sale of the Bathurst St. property,
the year in which it was sold and the following year.  In none of these financial
statements is there any amount shown for payment of a maintenance person or manager.
Further, there is no appreciable difference in the expenses shown for repairs
and maintenance in any of these years even though in 2002 the expenses were
with respect to only one property, the Bathurst St. property having been sold by then.

[
53
]

The
approach which Ms. Katz adopted in answering questions while on the witness
stand raises serious concerns as to the reliability of her evidence.  Although
she was pleasant and respectful, she was not a co-operative witness.  Often,
she would not concede the obvious or would concede it only after having proof
of it put to her.

[
54
]

Of greater
significance, however, is the direct evidence of Ms. Katz’s lack of
credibility. For example, in an affidavit she swore in 2005, she was adamant
that she did not receive any insurance proceeds following the death of her
mother.  However, subsequent to that affidavit being filed, Mr. Nimelman
learned that only nine months before swearing the affidavit, Ms. Katz had, as a
result of her mother’s death, received the proceeds of an insurance policy in
the amount of $33,000.  Ms. Katz admits that her affidavit was false.

[
55
]

Her sworn
financial statements provide further proof of Ms. Katz’s lack of credibility.
By way of example, her December 2001 financial statement fails to disclose the
existence of Orno, its assets or its income which in that year was $29,425.00,
though she is its sole shareholder and fails to disclose $30,000 in Canada
Savings Bonds purchased that year.

[
56
]

It was
not until her March 2005 financial statement filed in support of her motion for
interim spousal support that Ms. Katz first revealed the existence of Orno.
However, the revelation was of little assistance as the value shown was merely
“tbd”.  Nor did Ms. Katz include income resulting from the demutualization of
the Sun Life Insurance company.  She denied receiving this income, but it was
subsequently established that she had received it.  Further, she failed to
include her inheritance totalling $184,715, more than half of which she
received in 2006.  Her financial statement of November 2006 shows a debt of
$35,200 being a TD-Canada Trust line of credit.  However, this debt had been
paid off in October 2006.
[4]

[
57
]

Further
evidence of Ms. Katz’s lack of candour is her denial of having a trust fund for
Oren.  According to Mr. Nimelman, Oren had asked Ms. Katz to use some of the
proceeds of that fund to contribute to the private school fees for his last
year of high school.  Ms. Katz refused to contribute.  At trial she denied the
existence of such a fund and did not list it in her financial statement.
However, the trust fund is listed in a January 2006 statement of accounts held
by her through her mutual fund dealer. (Ms. Katz did not produce this statement
and apparently did not know that Mr. Nimelman had been provided with a copy of
it.)  Oren’s trust fund is stated to have a value $7,074.35.

[
58
]

There is
considerably more evidence of Ms. Katz’s lack of forthrightness.  For example,
in submitting that Mr. Nimelman was not forthcoming with his disclosure, Ms.
Katz pointed to the fact that he had failed to respond to her lawyer’s March 9,
2005 request for disclosure.  This is misleading.  While it is true that Mr.
Nimelman’s lawyer did not send a responding letter, Mr. Nimelman swore an
affidavit on March 15, 2005, filed in response to Ms. Katz’s motion, in which
the information sought by Ms. Murray was provided.

[
59
]

Ms. Katz
demonstrated that she could not be relied on to be forthcoming with relevant
and necessary evidence.  Further examples of this are set out below under the
heading “Disclosure.”

[
60
]

Her
pleadings in her actions arising out of the termination of her employment are a
further reflection of Ms. Katz’s unreliability.  She claims that she is
entitled to compensation for the difficulty in finding employment in light of
the damage to her reputation arising from the circumstance of her termination.
Yet, this pleading was drafted at the same time as she was taking the position
with her insurer that she was disabled as a result of her neurological
condition.

[
61
]

Mr.
Nimelman, like Ms. Katz, is capable and a committed parent.  I find him to have
given his evidence in a balanced and fair way without overstatement. When what
appeared to be inconsistencies in his evidence were put to him or when his
evidence appeared to be unreliable, he provided credible explanations.

[
62
]

In
giving his evidence, Mr. Nimelman complained of having a poor memory,
particularly in relation to the timing of things.  Consistent with this, he
sometimes struggled in his efforts to get the timing of events correct and was
confused or mistaken from time to time.  However, he readily acknowledged that
he might be wrong.  The result is that while the sequence of events as
described by him cannot always be taken to be correct, his credibility is not
impugned.

[
63
]

As
stated at the outset, where the evidence of Ms. Katz and Mr. Nimelman is in
conflict, I prefer the evidence of Mr. Nimelman, unless otherwise noted.
Further, where there is no corroberating evidence to support Ms. Katz’s
position, I find that she has failed to meet the onus of proving her claim.

[
64
]

It is
worth noting that while Ms. Katz and Mr. Nimelman were each critical of the
other, neither was antagonistic towards or disrespectful of the other.  This is
in spite of the hostility that this litigation has engendered. They are to be
commended for this.

DISCLOSURE

[
65

to

Family Law Act
.
(See
Hutchinson
, and
Novosel

v.
Novosel
(1999),
1999 CanLII 1291 (ON CA)
, 1R.F.L.(5
th

]

Hudson
v

v.
Kirk
(sub.n.m.
Kirk

[
124
]

There is no evidence of any step being taken by Ms. Katz in reliance

[
125
]

The case on which Ms. Katz relies in submitting that there has been
prejudice,
MacDonald
v.
MacDonald
(2000),

2000 CanLII 22594 (ON SC)
, 14 R.F.L. (5
th
)
135 (Ont. S.C.J.), is distinguishable as in that case there was clear evidence
of substantial prejudice.  The respondent had remarried and started a second
family relying on the fact that he had been divorced for 11 years without any

[
126
]

The onus is on Mr. Nimelman to satisfy the court that Ms. Katz will
not suffer substantial prejudice as a result of the delay in the bringing of
his equalization claim.  (
Douthwaite
v.
Douthwaite,
[1997] O.J.
No. 3427 at para. 33
)  In the absence of any evidence of prejudice to which to
respond, Mr. Nimelman has met that onus.

Conclusion

[
127
]

Here, as in
Novosel
, the parties continued to negotiate long
after the limitation period expired and no issue of prescription was raised
until long after the expiry of the limitation period.

[
128
]

While I recognise that limitation periods are there to be observed
and are important in bringing finality to matters and allowing parties to get
on with their lives, the
Family Law Act

acknowledges that in specified
circumstances the time limit should be extended.  In my opinion, this is one of
those circumstances.

129

household effects.  However, at the time, he was content with the way in which

entitled to but did not receive in the equalization calculations.  I agree with
Ms. Katz that the total of $7,200 shown on Mr. Nimelman’s net family property
statement should be allocated equally.

[
133
]

The only listings of Ms. Katz’s date of marriage assets are in the
financial statement she swore in 1996 and in the schedule appended to the 1998
draft agreement.  In 1996, she stated her property to have a value of
$311,301.07 on valuation day.  To this must be added the Spectrum investment in
the amount of $13,641.00 which she failed to disclose.

[
134
]

In both her 1996 financial statement and the 1998 schedule, Ms. Katz
claims a date of marriage amount for stocks, $40,000 in the former and $40,500
in the latter.  (It may be noteworthy that the latter is the same amount that
Ms. Katz attributes to the value of Mr. Nimelman’s Israeli apartment on
marriage.)  There is no evidence, either oral or documentary, in support of
either amount and no amount was claimed by Ms. Katz at trial in response to
these stocks having been excluded from Mr. Nimelman’s net family property
statement.  I therefore do not include any amount for marriage date stock
holdings in my calculations.

[
135
]

Similarly, there is no evidence with respect to the $5,000 claimed
for a car in the 1998 schedule, though absent from the 1996 financial
statement.  This, too, is excluded from my calculations.

[
136
]

Mr. Nimelman accepts Ms. Katz’s claim of having $1500 worth of
jewellery as at the date of marriage.

[
137
]

Mr. Nimelman submits that Ms. Katz must have had valuation date
assets which she has not disclosed.  He relies on the fact that in the four and
a quarter years following valuation date, Ms. Katz made investments totalling
over $233,000 without incurring debt in spite of having only $15,456.17 of
unaccounted for assets following the purchase of the Blythwood property and a
total income of approximately $363,000 over that period.  (Ms. Katz did not
produce her tax return for 1996. I am assuming an income equal to that earned
in 1997 for the purpose of this analysis.)

[
138
]

While Ms. Katz’s investments do raise questions about the
reliability of her evidence on the issue of her income, there is nothing more
than speculation to support the proposition that the source of funding of
post-separation investments was valuation day assets.  I do not attribute any
amount to Ms. Katz to reflect the unidentified and unancknowldeged assets which
Mr. Nimelman insists she must have had at the time of separation.

[
139
]

From Ms. Katz’s valuation date assets must be deducted her valuation
date debts.  In her 1996 financial statement, Ms. Katz claimed disposition
costs of her RRSP’s of 25% and capital gains totalling $35,000.  Ms. Katz does
not know what the reference to capital gains is and therefore it is
disregarded.  The parties have agreed that the appropriate amount for RRSP
disposition costs is 10%.  Each is entitled to claim a debt of 10% of the value
of their respective RRSPs.   The balance of the debts claimed by each is agreed
to.

(b) deductions and exclusions

[
140
]
In protesting the legitimacy of the amounts which Mr. Nimelman seeks
to deduct or exclude form his net family property, Ms. Katz points to the fact
that, with the exception of the Israeli apartment, none of the items he now
relies on appeared in the financial statement he filed in February 2002.  Mr.
Nimelman explains this omission as being a result of his having relied solely
on memory in completing the 2002 financial statement and not taking serious
steps to determine what he had owned at the time of marriage and its value
while he continued to believe that he and Ms. Katz would be able to settle.
Once it became apparent to him that settlement was not likely, Mr. Nimelman was
no longer willing to adopt a ‘broad brush’ perspective and took the necessary
steps to locate the documentation he needed to identify his time of marriage
assets.  I accept this explanation.

(i)

car, household items and
jewellery

[
141
]

Ms. Katz submits that Mr. Nimelman is not entitled to the exclusion
claimed for a car.  Based on the car having been left in Israel after they
moved to Canada, she says that
as of the date of marriage it was either owned jointly by Mr. Nimelman and his
mother or exclusively by his mother.  There is no dispute that the car was paid
for by Mr. Nimelman and was in his name.  I accept his evidence that he was at
the time of purchase, and as of the date of marriage less than a year later,
the car’s sole owner and that its date of marriage value was $21,113.

[
142
]

Mr. Nimelman claims $2,400 in household items, furniture and
jewellery.  While I do not doubt that Mr. Nimelman had assets of this kind, I
am not able to put any value on them in the absence of any evidence with
respect to of what they consisted and do not include this amount in my
calculations.

(ii) Israeli apartment

[
143
]

The deduction claimed for this apartment is greater than what was
claimed in Mr. Nimelman’s 2006 net family property statement.  The current
value claimed is based on a more careful analysis.  I find that $45,530, as
claimed, is a reasonable estimate of the value of the apartment as of the date
of marriage.

(iii) bank accounts

[
144
]

I am satisfied based on the documentation provided that as of the
date of marriage, Mr. Nimelman held the equivalent of $4,207.00 in his bank
accounts.

(iv) cash

[
145
]

Mr. Nimelman claims to have had the equivalent of $16,500 in cash at
the time of marriage.  This was not in a bank account.  He explains that
because of the extraordinary inflation rate in Israel at the time, he would exchange the pay he received into U.S. funds as a hedge against that
inflation.  However, Israeli bank accounts did not hold U.S. funds.  For that reason, the money was
not deposited.   I accept Mr. Nimelman’s evidence as to the amount of cash he
held on the date of marriage.

(iv) inheritance

[
146
]
Mr. Nimelman excludes $10,872 from his net family property on the
basis of its having been an inheritance which was used in its entirety to
purchase an RRSP.  I accept that the RRSP purchased by Mr. Nimelman in 1994
shortly after the inheritance was received was funded with the proceeds of the
inheritance.  Mr. Nimelman is therefore entitled to this exclusion.

Conclusion

[
147
]

Based on the above, and the agreed upon amounts as set out in the
attached Appendix A, I find that Ms. Katz owes Mr. Nimelman an equalization
payment of $77,590.00.

SPOUSAL
SUPPORT

[
148
]

Ms. Katz seeks spousal support from Mr. Nimelman of $1,500 a month,
retroactive to December 2001, the date of the issuance of her claim.

[
149
]

She submits that she is entitled to this support based on the
consequences of the roles assumed by the parties during their marriage, the
consequences Ms. Katz has suffered as a result of the behaviour of Mr.
Nimelman, and on her need and Mr. Nimelman’s ability to pay.

[
150
]

It is Mr. Nimelman’s position that she is not entitled to support
based on her current circumstances.

History
of Claim

[
151
]

In August 1996, Ms. Katz’s settlement proposal as set out in the
draft agreement forwarded to Mr. Nimelman was that “neither party will ever
have to pay spousal support to the other…”  The next draft was prepared in 1998
after Ms. Katz stopped working.  In it, she sought an acknowledgement of her
unemployment and inability to work, did not seek spousal support but did
propose that she retain her right to seek support in the future.  The petition
for divorce, which she filed a little over three years later, claimed support.

[
152
]

The next draft settlement agreement prepared on behalf of Ms. Katz,
the 2002 draft, again proposed that spousal support be left open, but this time
the proposal was that it be kept open by way of Mr. Nimelman paying $100
monthly, which amount would be reviewed in the event of a material change in
circumstances.

[
153
]

As of her 2002 settlement proposal, Ms. Katz did not consider herself
to require spousal support.  That remained the case until she was no longer
entitled to child support with respect to Oren.  In her affidavit filed in
support of her March 2005 motion for interim spousal support, Ms. Katz stated
that while she was receiving child support for both children, her net
disposable income was the same as Mr. Nimelman’s.

[
154
]

Ms. Katz took no steps to pursue either spousal support or a final
agreement until Oren moved in with Mr. Nimelman in January 2005 and Mr.
Nimelman stopped making his child support payments.  She claims that she
considered the support she was receiving to have a component of spousal support
in it and for that reason was content not to pursue a written agreement
confirming her entitlement to spousal support.  This is not borne out by the
evidence.  Correspondence from Ms. Murray makes it clear that the support was
based exclusively on the amount owing pursuant to the child support guidelines.

[
155
]

Ms. Katz served materials for a motion for interim spousal and child
support.  The result of that motion was an order requiring Mr. Nimelman to pay
child support for Noah who continued to live with Ms. Katz, net of her child
support obligations for Oren and a dismissal of the motion for interim spousal
support.  At the time, the expectation was that the trial would take place in
less than a year.

[
156
]

As a result of Oren living with Mr. Nimelman, Ms. Katz received
$471.00 less than she had previously after taking into account the $500 monthly
which she estimated she saved as a result of Oren no longer living with her.

Law

[
157
]

Spousal support is governed by the
Divorce Act
,
R.S.C. 1985,
c. 3 (2d Supp.), as am.

Section 15.2(4) sets out the factors to be
considered in making a spousal support order:

Factors

(4)          In
making an order under subsection (1) or an interim order under

subsection
(2), the court shall take into consideration the condition,

means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse, including:

(a) the length of time the spouses
cohabited;

(b) the functions performed by
each spouse during cohabitation; and

(c) any order, agreement or
arrangement relating to support of either

spouse.

[
158
]

Those factors are to be weighed in the context of the objectives of
spousal support as set out in s. 15.2(6):

Objectives of spousal support order

(6)   An order made under subsection (1) or an
interim order under subsection

(2) that provides for the support of a
spouse should

(a)    recognize any economic advantages or
disadvantages to the spouses

arising from the marriage or its
breakdown;

(b)   apportion between the spouses any
financial consequences arising

from the care of any child of
the marriage over and above any

obligation for the support of
any child of the marriage;

(c)
relieve any economic hardship of the spouses arising from the

breakdown of the marriage; and

(d)   in so far as practicable, promote
the economic self-sufficiency of each

spouse within a reasonable
period of time.

[
159
]

In considering the application of the above provisions of the
Divorce
Act
to the facts of this case, I am guided by the principles set out in
Bracklow

v.
Bracklow,
1999 CanLII 715 (SCC)
, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 420.  These include:

(a)

all three models for support, compensatory, non-compensatory and
contractual,

must be considered in deciding on entitlement (para. 37);

(b)

need alone may justify an award of spousal support (para. 43);

(c)

the obligation of support is a result of the relationship
established through

marriage and the expectations that may reasonably flow from it (para.
44);

and

(d)

whether support should be awarded ultimately depends on what is
just and fair

in the circumstances (para. 48).

[
160
]

Some of the
Divorce Act

objectives have been conceded to have
no application.  Ms. Katz was self-sufficient at the time of the marriage
breakdown; she has not submitted that she has suffered economic hardship
arising from the breakdown of the marriage; and, has not submitted that there
has been any economic disadvantage to her or advantage to Mr. Nimelman as a
result of the marriage breakdown.

Analysis

(a)
length of marriage

[
161
]

Given its ten-year duration, this was a medium length marriage.
When Ms. Katz first moved for spousal support, the parties had been separated
as long as they had been married.

(b) the roles of the parties

[
162
]

Ms. Katz claims that she bore the burden of child care during the
marriage.  In this context, she gives as an example her alone having the
responsibility for driving Oren to and from Bialik while he was in
kindergarten, something which was indisputably burdensome.  However, the
decision to undertake this burden was hers and was one which cannot objectively
be viewed as justified based on the evidence.

[
163
]

Her evidence with respect to the relative time she and Mr. Nimelman
spent with the children is contradicted by Mr. Nimelman.  I accept his evidence
that in the normal course, there was no significant distinction between their
child care responsibilities.  However, there were periods when Mr. Nimelman was
involved in projects that did require him to work longer than normal hours.  But,
this did not cause economic disadvantage to Ms. Katz and is not a factor that
on its own would justify an award of spousal support.

[
164
]

Ms. Katz submits that she suffered economic disadvantage because in
order to spend more time with the children, she gave up a lucrative private
practice for less remunerative work.  This is not supported by evidence.  Ms.
Katz felt that having two young children at home did not lessen her
effectiveness at work.  There is no evidence that Mr. Nimelman asked her to
reduce her hours.  And, there is no evidence as to what her financial prospects
at Baker & McKenzie might have been if she had stayed and therefore no
basis for a finding that there was any economic disadvantage resulting from her
move to the College of Family
Physicians.

[
165
]

For the ten years following separation, Ms. Katz had custody of both
children.  There is no evidence, however, that this has caused her any economic
disadvantage.  Her position is that she has been unable to be in the workforce
since the end of 1997.  Further, a condition for the continuation of her long
term disability benefits is that she earn no income.

(b) prior agreements or orders

[
166
]

As stated above, there was a ten year history of no spousal support
being paid or sought.  Ms. Katz’s motion in the spring of 2005 for interim
support was unsuccessful.

(c) Mr. Nimelman’s behaviour

[
167
]

In reliance on the Supreme Court of Canada decision in
Leskun
v.
Leskun
,
2006 SCC 25 (CanLII)
, [2006] S.C.J. No. 25,
Ms. Katz submits the consequences of Mr. Nimelman’s behaviour have been such as
to entitle her to spousal support.

[
168
]

In 1998 Ms. Katz bought two rental properties. The purpose, she
says, was to supplement her income and to accumulate capital on which she could
rely when her disability payments stopped at age 65.  She formed Orno, a
company in which she intended to hold her rental properties.  She submits that
the fact that Orno is not financially successful is Mr. Nimelman’s fault.  She
says that because she constantly had to manage the consequences of his conduct,
her energies were diverted from Orno.

[
169
]

Ms. Katz relies on the January 2005 incident when Oren moved in with
Mr. Nimelman.  I accept Mr. Nimelman’s version of the events, not only because,
as I have said, where their evidence differs I accept his, but also because it
is bolstered by the evidence of Ms. Goldberg as well as Mr. Nimelman’s January
21, 2005 e-mail sent to Ms. Katz demanding an adjustment to the child support
he was paying.

[
170
]

It is true that when Oren moved in with Mr. Nimelman, he stopped
paying child support.  I accept Mr. Nimelman’s evidence that this had not been
his intention, but was a response, admittedly wrong, to Ms. Katz’s refusal to
agree to a reduced amount of support to reflect the change in circumstances.
Mr. Nimelman’s behaviour in withholding all support is inexcusable.  However,
in just over three months, the arrears were made up and payments reinstated.

[
171
]

In support of her position, Ms. Katz points to what she says was Mr.
Nimelman’s unilateral decision to enrol Oren and Noah in a school close to his
home after the family moved out of the matrimonial home and to Mr. Nimelman’s
dealings with the Heschel School.  She submits these things amount to
misconduct on the part of Mr. Nimelman which contributed to the depletion of
her energy.  However, I reject her views regarding the events on which she
relies in favour of Mr. Nimelman’s as detailed above under the heading
“Background”.

[
172
]

I find there is no credible evidence of misconduct on the part of
Mr. Nimelman. I do not accept that his conduct created crises and damage that Ms.
Katz was required to solve or ameliorate.

[
173
]

Ms. Katz submits that Mr. Nimelman abused the disclosure provisions
of the
Family Law Rules.
She says that his demands for disclosure were
abusive and resulted in the further depletion of her energies and the delay of
this trial by almost two and a half years.  This, in turn, resulted in
increasing financial hardship and stress.  However, the evidence does not
support her interpretation of Mr. Nimelman’s disclosure demands.  The issue of
disclosure is discussed above under the heading “Disclosure”.

[
174
]

The only evidence as to what Ms. Katz would have been able to do in
relation to Orno, or what she would have done differently had her energies not
been diverted as she claims, is with respect to the sale of the Bathurst St.
property.  I have found, however, that this assertion is not credilbe.  (See
above, under the heading “Credibility”.)

[
175
]

In
Leskun
,
the court held that the behaviour of a spouse may
be relevant to the factors to be considered in determining the right to support
and its duration and amount.  However, Ms. Katz has not established any relevant
misconduct on the part of Mr. Nimelman. The decision in
Leskun

has no
application to this case.

(d)  need

[
176
]

This leaves the question of whether non-compensatory factors provide
a basis for an award of support.  Need alone, if it can be established, may be
sufficient basis for requiring the payment of spousal support, where the payor
has the ability to pay.
[8]

[
177
]

Ms. Katz’s need, if it can be demonstrated, arises from a disability
that developed following the breakdown of the marriage.  That fact does not
alter the potential support obligation of Mr. Nimelman
[9]
;   nor
does the fact that in the absence of a support payment, it is not likely that
Ms. Katz will become a burden of the state.  I do not accept Mr. Nimelman’s
submission that the reasoning in
Bracklow

is limited to cases where the
alternative to a support award is state support of the support claimant.  That
approach reflects too narrow an interpretation of the court’s reasoning,
particularly in light of its emphasis on seeking a result that is just and
fair.

[
178
]

In determining whether need alone is a sufficient basis for awarding
support, I must consider the expectations of Ms. Katz and Mr. Nimelman that
flowed from their marriage and the circumstances in which the need arose.

[
179
]

Ms. Katz was the primary earner throughout the marriage.  Though
they owed each other a duty of support, theirs was an ‘independent’ model of
marriage to the extent that each was financially self-sufficient.  If there was
any expectation of support, it would be on Mr. Nimelman’s side.  However, he
neither wished nor sought support.  There was nothing in the marriage that
would create an expectation of ongoing support for Ms. Katz.

[
180
]

Based on Ms. Katz’s proposed settlements and her failure to take any
steps to obtain support, she did not consider herself to be in need until many
years after she became disabled.  Indeed, for a number of years, she was able
to support herself financially, in spite of her disability, at a level close to
what she had earned when employed.  In addition to her disability benefits, she
earned rent from the apartment in her basement and from the rental properties
she purchased in 1998 as well as interest income from a number of investments.
In 2001, her income was close to $90,000 on her own evidence and may have been
higher.  Her income was very close to Mr. Nimelman’s.

[
181
]

Ms. Katz’s income subsequently decreased.  This was a result of her
decision not to continue renting out the basement apartment and her sale of the
rental property.  It was not reduced as a result of the marriage or its
breakdown and not because of her disability, but rather because of decisions
she made that were unrelated to either the marriage or the disability.

[
182
]

Ms. Katz last rented her basement apartment in 2002-2003.  She was
receiving rent of $1,050 monthly.  She gives three reasons for no longer
renting it: she had a bad experience with a tenant which has left her feeling
that it is not appropriate for her to rent the apartment; the restriction on
her access to the laundry facilities resulting from having a tenant is
inconvenient; and, her lease precludes the rental.  I do not accept any of
these reasons.  She successfully rented the apartment after the negative
experience she relies on; the laundry problem could be resolved at minimal
cost; and, there is no evidence that her landlord would object to the leasing
of the apartment (the landlord did not previously object, but may not have know
about it) and based on a reasonable interpretation, the lease is not an
impediment to the apartment being rented. Accordingly, in the event of need,
income from this apartment would be available to Ms. Katz.

[
183
]

It was not until Ms. Katz lost the benefit of child support for Oren
that she claimed to have need.  Mr. Nimelman submits that if the loss of the
approximately $500 net a month has resulted in Ms. Katz having need, then that
need should not entitle her to spousal support as she has created it. This is
because Oren would have continued to live with her had she not forced him out.
Mr. Nimelman submits that Ms. Katz, not he, should bear the consequences of her
having done so.  While I accept that Ms. Katz did tell Oren that he had to
leave and was not to return, I do not agree that this means that her resulting
financial circumstances must be disregarded.  Given the evidence as to the
tension between Ms. Katz and Oren, it seems that it was not in Oren’s best
interests to continue to live with Ms. Katz.  The method by which the change in
residence was accomplished does not alter that fact. It is not a factor in
considering entitlement.

(i)

income

and expenses

[
184
]

Ms. Katz relies on her June 12, 2007 financial statement to
establish her need.  However, the information contained in this statement is
not reliable.  In completing this statement, Ms. Katz relied on her 2005 income
tax return.
[10]

Her explanation for doing so is that she could not afford to have her 2006
return prepared.  I do not consider this to be a credible explanation.  Her
failure to provide current information is unjustified and leads to the adverse
inference that a current return would have shown income in an amount higher
than in 2005.

[
185
]

Ms. Katz submits that her current income from all sources is
$65,684.  With this income, she claims a monthly deficit of $1481.56.
[11]

[
186
]

Mr. Nimelman submits that neither her alleged annual income nor
alleged expenses are accurate.  He maintains that she must have undisclosed
sources of income as her net worth continues to increase.

[
187
]

For the purposes of determining her entitlement to spousal support,
Ms. Katz submits that because Orno, the company she established in 1998, is a
separate corporate entity, it should not be taken into account. On that basis,
according to Ms. Katz, if the Hopewell property produced a profit, that profit should not be included in
Ms. Katz’s income.  Her position is weakened by the fact that in spite of the Hopewell property being reported as owned
by Orno, title to it is actually in Ms. Katz’s name.  But, even setting that
aside, I do not accept Ms. Katz’s position.

[
188
]

Ms. Katz is the sole shareholder of Orno.  She says she set up the
company to hold her real estate holdings and take advantage of what she
believed would be available tax benefits.
[12]
On
cross-examination, she admitted that she sometimes deposited rental income in
her personal account (and did not tell her accountant) and that she did not
distinguish between her personal and business expenses.

[
189
]

There is no question that Orno and Ms. Katz are one and the same and
that Ms. Katz is the beneficial owner of any property held by Orno.  As stated
by the Court of Appeal in
Wildman v.Wildman
,
2006 CanLII 33540 (ON CA)
, [2006] O.J. No. 3966 (C.A.), corporate arrangements must not be
permitted to work an injustice in family law.  If it were necessary, this would
clearly be an appropriate case in which to pierce the corporate veil.

[
190
]

The Orno financial statements show an average annual loss of around
$4,900 beginning in 2002, following the sale of the Bathurst
St. property.  However the financial statements are
not reliable.  They are based exclusively on information provided by Ms. Katz
to her accountant who did not verify the accuracy of that information and did
not enquire as to the legitimacy of the expenses claimed.  Had he done so, he
would not have included at least a portion of the claimed amounts.  Not all of
the rent received is reflected in the statements as, as stated above, on
occasion Ms. Katz deposited rent cheques in her personal account instead of the
Orno account.  In addition, the most recent statement is unreliable because it
is based on information that is not current and significant expenses are
claimed for work that is allegedly intended but has not been done. I draw an
adverse inference against Ms. Katz based on her failure to provide current
evidence with respect to Orno.

[
191
]

The only reliable evidence as to the earnings of Hopewell is that of Mr. David Zucker, a
chartered accountant called on behalf Mr. Nimelman.  Mr. Zuker reviewed the
Orno source documents to determine whether Orno/ the Hopewell property was in a profit or deficit position.  I accept his
evidence that for the period ending February 28, 2007, the Hopewell property was in a positive
position and had rental income for the year of $12,472.85, net of expenses.
This amount must be included in Ms. Katz’s income in assessing her need.

[
192
]

There was evidence from both Ms. Katz’s accountant and from Mr.
Zuker regarding the deductions claimed by Orno.  The concern for the purposes
of this claim is not their propriety from a tax perspective, but rather their
significance in terms of Ms. Katz’s personal finances.

[
193
]

Some of Ms. Katz personal expenses, expenses claimed in her
financial statement were paid for by Orno.  Ms. Katz’s telephone, her car
insurance, maintenance and gas, her meals outside the home and the Blythwood
mortgage were charged to and paid by Orno.  To that extent that Orno is being
used to finance the personal expenses shown on Ms. Katz’s budget, her expenses
are overstated.  To the same extent, these personal expenses reduce Orno’s
income.  In spite of the loss stated for tax purposes, Orno represents a source
of income for Ms. Katz.

[
194
]

Orno’s significance in this action goes beyond its representing a
source of income for Ms. Katz’s.  Orno is of importance as a result of Ms.
Katz’s initial failure to disclose it and then her subsequent failure to
provide any information regarding its value.  This, understandably, created and
fuelled Mr. Nimelman’s mistrust of the disclosure which he was receiving.

[
195
]

Ms. Katz’s expenses as set out in her 2007 financial statement are
not accurate.   She includes amounts paid by Orno and includes medical expenses
which she has not incurred.
[13]
Based on her budget as shown in her financial statements filed over
the years, Ms. Katz should have accumulated a deficit of around $500,000,
exclusive of legal fees.  However, the debt she lists is $272,792.00, inclusive
of at least $47,122 in legal fees owing.

[
196
]

This is explained, Ms. Katz submits, in part by her having used the
$100,000 which she received in December of last year as an advance on her
inheritance.  She says that she used this money to pay off debt including legal
fees and for living expenses.  For the reasons discussed below under the
heading ‘debt and other liabilities’ I do not accept that this money was used
to pay down all but a small amount of debt and Ms. Katz’s living expenses,
based on her own numbers, could not be a significant draw on those funds. Ms.
Katz’s explanation is not reasonable.

[
197
]

Ms. Katz has admitted that she has overstated some of the expenses
listed in her financial statement.  Some of the expenses on their face appear
excessive.  Others are no longer being incurred.  None are supported by
documentation.

[
198
]

Ms. Katz has discretionary expenses that can be eliminated.  For
example, she is paying $121.83 a month for a policy of life insurance which
will result in a payout to her should Mr. Nimelman die and a payout to Mr. Nimelman
should Ms. Katz predecease him.  Mr. Nimelman has said that he has no interest
in having this insurance.  As the children are provided for through insurance
paid for by Ms. Katz’s disability insurer, this expense is unnecessary.

[
199
]

Ms. Katz concedes that to the extent that her need results from
costs incurred in pursuing the wrongful dismissal actions, it does not justify
an award of spousal support.  The only evidence of those costs is of the
$35,000 paid in October 2004 as a retainer for the trial.  Clearly, she will
have spent very substantially more than that in reaching the trial stage of the
actions.

[
200
]

Mr. Nimelman takes the position that the court should disregard the
fact that once a divorce is granted, Ms. Katz will have increased expenses
because she will no longer have the benefit of his medical plan.  To take this
into account, he submits, is inconsistent with the requirement that support is
to be considered on the basis of the parties circumstances at the time of the

immediately on the issuance of this judgment is to do a disservice to the

unknown beyond the fact that they are currently claimed at $920 monthly.

[
201
]

I recognise that in considering Ms. Katz’s expenses, I have not
taken into account necessary tax gross ups.  However, to do so is neither
necessary because they would be insufficient to result in a change to my

(ii)  assets, debts and liabilities

[
202
]

In spite of the returns on her RRSP and RSP’s being consistently
low, the total value of Ms. Katz’s investments has substantially increased.

[
203
]

Mr. Nimelman is convinced that Ms. Katz has investments which she
has not revealed.  He bases this belief not only on the fact that Ms. Katz’s
disclosure of assets has been unreliable (this is discussed above under the
heading “Disclosure”) but on Ms. Katz’s failure to provide evidence as to how

]

Ms. Katz has RRSP’s and an RSP totalling $362,000 as of June 12,

]

]

approximately $82,000 of the $100,000
[14]
.  As a

,

29
).

]

210
]

]

the value shown for 79 Blythwood is $164,000,

]

]

has made improvements to the property.

214
]

Even if I were to accept that Ms. Katz must spend money on repairs
to the house, as she claims, that would not change my view that the house has a

215
]

Ms. Katz will shortly receive the balance of her inheritance in the
amount of $76,500 less one-third of estate administration costs.  Although

father’s estate has failed to do so.  The administrator is Ms. Katz’s brother.

costs for the purposes of this trial.  In the absence of an agreed to number I
infer, based on the failure of Ms. Katz’s brother to provide the necessary
information, that it is not substantial.

[
216
]

Although the net proceeds remaining from Ms. Katz’s inheritance
should have been included in Ms. Katz’s financial statement, I do not take them
into account in determining Ms. Katz’s entitlement to spousal support. This is
because of my finding that she is required to make an equalization payment to
Mr. Nimelman in a roughly equal amount.

[
217
]

Ms. Katz refused to provide Mr. Nimelman with access to
documentation regarding the account into which the proceeds of the sale of the
Bathurst St. property and which have not been accounted for were deposited and

closed account were dispersed.  I draw an adverse inference from these refusals
to disclose, as I do with respect to all of Ms. Katz’s refusals.  That
inference leads to the conclusion that the funds continue to be held, in one
form or another, by Ms. Katz and, as such, either are producing income or ought
to be.

(e)
Mr. Nimelman’s ability to pay

[
218
]

Mr. Nimelman’s means must be considered in determining Ms. Katz’s
entitlement to spousal support from him.

[
219
]

His 2007 earnings will be $106,705.44.   His main assets are his
condominium which he values at $199,000 and over $360,000 in RRSP’s.
Additionally, he has savings of just over $20,000, $15,000 of which is in a
savings account earning 3.5% interest.  He intends to put this money towards
the down payment of a condominium that would provide him with more room than his

[
220
]

Mr. Nimelman claims a monthly deficit of nearly $1,300.  A
significant portion of that consists of Oren’s university expenses and includes
the costs of such things as a laptop computer, which will not be an annual expense.
The university related expenses have been incurred only since September of this
year.  Even if Ms. Katz were contributing to the costs of these expenses on a
proportionate basis, Mr. Nimelman would still be in a deficit position based on
his budget.

[
221
]

Ms. Katz takes issue with Mr. Nimelman’s budget, primarily disputing
the amount he spends on his trips to Israel and on his RRSP’s.  She submits that in considering his means for
the purposes of spousal support, these expenses should be disregarded as they
represent a discretionary reduction in his means.

[
222
]

In each year for which documentation has been provided by Ms. Katz,
she has invested in a RRSP.  It seems reasonable to me that both spouses should
be maximising their RRSP contributions as they will be, in Ms. Katz’s case, a
primary source of income after age 65, and for Mr. Nimelman, the sole source of
income after his retirement.  Unlike Ms. Katz, Mr. Nimelman has no capital on
which to draw and no continuing source of income.  Their respective retirement
savings plans are in roughly the same amount, assuming Ms. Katz’s current
financial statement includes whatever RRSP contribution she may have made in
2006, an assumption which cannot be relied on.  Ms. Katz’s current net worth is
substantially higher than Mr. Nimelman’s.  It is not the intent of the support
provisions of the
Divorce Act

that Mr. Nimelman be required to forgo
reasonable planning for his retirement so as to support a spouse whose post
retirement financial circumstances are better than his.

[
223
]

I have found that it was a condition of Mr. Nimelman’s agreement to
move to Canada that he and the family return to Israel regularly.  Since then, Mr. Nimelman has usually made two trips
annually. He now visits his mother in January for her birthday and takes the
children with him on a visit in the summer. He continues to be committed to his
family in Israel. The costs of
the trips are substantial, in 2006 totalling $10,200. They are made up
primarily of air fare and car rental, as most of the time in Israel is spent staying with family.

[
224
]

Mr. Nimelman does not consider these trips to be vacations in that
he does not view them as discretionary.  I consider it to be in Oren and Noah’s
interests that they continue their relationship with their paternal grandmother
who is in her eighties (Mr. Nimelman’s father passed away in 2005) and the rest
of Mr. Nimelman’s family.  While the costs represent a substantial percentage
of Mr. Nimelman’s income, Ms. Katz, through her agreement to the trips at the
outset, acknowledged their importance to Mr. Nimelman.  If anything, they could
be expected to take on even greater importance on the breakdown of the
marriage.  They are reasonable in the circumstances.  In any event, increasing
Mr. Nimelman’s means by the cost of these trips would not have the result,
given all of the other relevant considerations, of creating a support
obligation for Mr. Nimelman.

[
225
]

It is necessary to consider the relative circumstances of the
parties.  Ms. Katz acknowledged that she and Mr. Nimelman had approximately
equal net disposable incomes before the child support she received was reduced
by a net amount of just under $500 in 2005.
[15]
The
differential after this reduction is not so substantial as to warrant, on its
own, payment of spousal support by Mr. Nimelman nor does Ms. Katz claim support
on that basis.  In any event, it would have to be considered in the context of
the living conditions of each.

[
226
]

Ms. Katz’s housing expenses, including water, electricity and
heating total $2175.86.  Mr. Nimelman’s expenses for the same items total
$692.98.  Their housing is vastly different. Ms. Katz lives in a well
furnished, two-storey detached house in a good residential neighbourhood.  Mr.
Nimelman lives in a basic, two bedroom condominium in a less desirable
location.

[
227
]

Mr. Nimelman submits that in considering his circumstances it is
necessary to take into account the fact that he does not have job security.
Since the completion of a major project at work, his responsibilities have been
limited to business development. His employer has recently offered early
retirement options and leaves of absence to employees in an effort to deal with
the work shortage the company has for some time been experiencing.  This
follows rounds of layoffs of employees.

[
228
]

Ms. Katz maintains that Mr. Nimelman should find another job.  He,
however, says that this is not practical as there is no other employer in Canada at which he could work in the field
in which he has developed his expertise.  Any job he might take would be at a
significantly lower income.  I accept Mr. Nimelman’s evidence on this and that
what makes most sense for him is to continue in his efforts to rebuild his
company’s business.

[
229
]

While I recognise the insecurity of Mr. Nimelman’s employment, it is
not a factor in my decision.  In deciding whether Ms. Katz is entitled to
support, it is Mr. Nimelman’s current circumstances that I must consider unless
there is certainty of a future outcome.

Conclusion

[
230
]

I have concluded that Ms. Katz has not established need.  Bearing in
mind the provisions of
s. 15
of the
Divorce Act
,
and the guiding
principles set out in
Bracklow
, the result is that Ms. Katz is not
entitled to spousal support.

[
231
]

Ms. Katz has not been candid about what she has done with monies she
has received and has failed to make disclosure that has been ordered or
requested with respect to accounts she has had.  The adverse inference I draw
from this together with the fact that her net worth has continued to increase,
brings me to the conclusion that Ms. Katz has undisclosed assets and income.

[
232
]

As well, Ms. Katz has the ability to earn additional income.  She
must look to her own potential sources of income and take all reasonable steps
to maximize her income before turning to Mr. Nimelman for support. She can eliminate
the corporate structure through which she operates the Hopewell property to take advantage of the tax benefits that would result.
She can rent out her basement apartment to obtain rental income
[16]
which would then provide her with tax benefits resulting from the
ability to deduct a portion of her housing expenses, as she did in the past. If
she does not wish to rent out the basement apartment, she can reduce her
expenses by obtaining less costly housing.

[
233
]

Although I do not give this significant weight in my consideration
of Ms. Katz’s need, I note that her wrongful dismissal claims remain
outstanding.  Based on her willingness to proceed to trial when the action was
first called and the fact that nothing has changed since that time, I assume
that Ms. Katz believes that her claim is meritorious and should result in her
receiving some payment.  She has not indicated otherwise though given the
opportunity to do so. It is reasonable to assume, therefore, that once this
matrimonial action is finalized, Ms. Katz will revive the wrongful actions with
the expectation of obtaining money through them.

[
234
]

Noah continues to live with Ms. Katz.  Oren lives with Mr. Nimelman,

]

]

]

240
]

]

]

]

]

]
